query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A carefully calibrated single-step flash annealing treatment applied to the as-cast eutectic HEA will promote targeted nano-scale segregation (e.g., of Cr) at the internal phase boundaries, thereby transforming semi‐coherent interfaces into chemically strengthened, more coherent boundaries. This change will mitigate dislocation pile-ups and delay local stress concentrations and microcrack nucleation, leading to improved room-temperature tensile ductility while retaining or even increasing overall strength.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a hierarchical dual‐phase lamellar microstructure composed of L12 (ductile) and B2 (hard) colonies.
generation.intervention: A single-step rapid 'flash' annealing treatment (i.e. rapid heating to an optimized intermediate temperature for a short duration followed by rapid quenching) designed to induce enhanced segregation of beneficial solutes (such as Cr) at the phase boundaries.
generation.conditions: Processing and subsequent mechanical testing at room temperature under quasi-static tensile loading. The flash anneal must be optimized to promote interfacial segregation without coarsening the lamellae or altering the bulk phase volume fractions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of ultra‐thin, Cr-enriched interfacial layers that modify the local atomic structure and bonding of the semi‐coherent phase boundaries, turning them into effective dislocation sinks.
generation.mechanism: During the flash anneal, accelerated diffusion drives selective solute segregation toward the phase boundaries. The resulting chemically modified boundaries possess higher local cohesion and altered lattice mismatch, which impedes excessive dislocation pile-ups. By reducing local stress concentrations, these interfaces can delay microcrack initiation while the dual-phase architecture continues to provide precipitation and barrier strengthening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the flash annealed alloy will exhibit a measurable improvement in room-temperature tensile ductility (e.g., an increase in elongation to failure) without a reduction in, and possibly even with an enhancement of, yield and ultimate tensile strengths.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic HEA typically shows limited tensile ductility and brittle behavior due to dislocation pile-ups at semi-coherent phase boundaries, despite having a respectable strength, as reported in studies (e.g., yield strength ~750–1165 MPa with elongations around 18%).
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only if the flash annealing time and temperature are precisely controlled: over-annealing could lead to unwanted phase coarsening or transformation, while insufficient treatment may fail to induce adequate interfacial segregation.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the observations of nano-scale Cr segregation at phase boundaries (PMC6175879::web::013::discussion) and the strengthening effects of nano-precipitates (PMC6478865::web::000::abstract) to a new regime where targeted interfacial chemistry is tuned to mitigate dislocation pile-ups. The new aspect is the use of a single-step flash annealing process specifically calibrated to enhance interfacial segregation, whose optimal parameters and corresponding structural‐performance correlation remain to be experimentally determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples from the same as-cast ingot. Subject one set to the optimized flash annealing treatment and leave the other untreated. Characterize the interfacial chemistry using atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution TEM to quantify the presence and uniformity of Cr (or chosen solute) segregation at the phase boundaries. Then, perform room-temperature tensile tests (quasi-static loading) and use in-situ imaging techniques (e.g., digital image correlation combined with high-resolution microscopy) to track dislocation activity and microcrack initiation in both sets.
measurements: APT and TEM data showing the extent of Cr-enrichment at phase boundaries.
Tensile stress-strain curves quantifying yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure.
Observations of dislocation pile-up densities and microcrack initiation sites near the interfaces.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the flash annealed samples do not exhibit statistically significant Cr enrichment at the interfaces or if the mechanical testing shows no improvement (or a degradation) in ductility and/or strength compared to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis that the flash annealing treatment mitigates dislocation pile-ups and improves ductility is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The properties of many metallic alloys are essentially related to the structure, morphology and chemical distribution of boundaries. In terms of atomic structure, the phase boundaries contained in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were supposed to be insufficient in prohibiting dislocations due to their semi-coherent nature, which is similar to those widely reported in NiAl dual-phase intermetallic alloys,. However, in-situ deformation tests revealed that dense dislocation storage can be achieved within FCC phases and dislocation walls were formed along phase boundaries. The unexpected strong interfaces are thought to be highly related to the chemically disordered distribution of multiple solution atoms at phase boundaries as well as in the matrix of HEAs. Particularly, an ultra-thin segregation zone of randomly distributed Cr atoms, typically less than 2 nm in width (Fig. 3b and S4), was detected near the phase boundary without forming complex intermetallic compounds, which were intrinsically brittle and would lead to stress concentration. Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading. Due to the fine lamellar microstructure with a large number of fcc-bcc interfaces, the alloy show relatively high flow-stresses, ~1400 MPa under quasi-static loading and in excess of 1800 MPa under dynamic loading.
